drapeaux.note: The French heading « Le retournement, cinq ans plus tard » (“The Reversal, Five Years Later”) does not fit the dates in the text, 1977 then 1983 (six years), nor the card punchline « en six ans » (“in six years”). Both figures are kept as in the French; the French needs a check.

titre: Darwin's Finches, Natural Selection Caught in the Act
accroche: On a Galápagos islet with no fresh water, a team has measured every finch, one by one, since 1973. A drought shows them evolution in real time.
contenu_vulgarise:
Daphne Major is a small volcanic cone in the Galápagos, with no freshwater source and no easy landing beach, home to only a handful of bird species. Since 1973, biologists Peter and Rosemary Grant, then their students, have captured, banded, and measured every medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) on the island: the population there is small enough to be counted in its entirety, rather than estimated from a sample. Natural selection is usually thought of as a process too slow to observe within a human lifetime. Daphne Major gave this team the opposite opportunity.

## A Drought That Sorts the Population

In 1977, the rains almost entirely fail. The soft, small seeds the finches usually eat grow scarce, and only the tough, spiny fruits of Tribulus remain abundant. Nearly 85% of the island's medium ground finch population starves to death within a few months. The sorting is not random: the birds with the largest beaks, able to crack these hard seeds, survive in a markedly higher proportion than the others. Peter Boag, then on the island, and Peter Grant document this result in Science in 1981: the average beak size of the population measured after the drought is larger than before, in a single generation, with no new gene introduced. This is natural selection itself, measured in the field rather than inferred from reasoning about geological time.

## The Reversal, Five Years Later

In 1983, an El Niño episode turns the tables. Abundant rains make the plants with small, soft seeds bloom again, and they once more become the most available resource. The advantage then changes sides: smaller, finer beaks make it possible to husk these seeds faster, and it is now the smallest birds that survive and reproduce best. The population's average beak size comes back down, in the same population, followed by the same team, through the same mechanism applied in the other direction.

## What This Shifts

The case of Daphne Major does not merely show that natural selection exists: it shows that it can reverse direction from one decade to the next, with an unpredictable climate, without either direction being right by nature. A large-beaked finch is not better adapted than a small-beaked one in the absolute: it is only so as long as hard seeds dominate. Followed over several decades, this population oscillates several times rather than converging on an ideal form, which led the Grants to describe their own results, in a later paper, as unpredictable evolution: predictable in the short term from the selection under way, unpredictable in the long term because the environment dictating it is not predictable.

repere.texte: During the 1977 drought on the islet of Daphne Major (Galápagos), nearly 85% of the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis) population starves to death within a few months; the birds with the largest beaks, able to break the tough seeds of the Tribulus that remained available, survive at a markedly higher rate.
repere.source: Ahmed, Farooq, “Profile of Peter R. Grant,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 107(13), 5703-5705, 2010

carte.punch: On a Galápagos islet, a team watched natural selection reverse direction in six years.
carte.idee: Since 1973, the Grants have measured every medium ground finch on the islet of Daphne Major. The 1977 drought kills 85% of the population and favors large beaks; the 1983 El Niño reverses the advantage toward small beaks: the same population shows natural selection at work in both directions.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Unpredictable Evolution in a 30-Year Study of Darwin's Finches (abstract, Grant & Grant, Science, 2002)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: Summary of thirty years of monitoring the same population: several documented reversals of selection, and the authors' conclusion on the unpredictable nature of long-term evolution.

quiz.question: What, in the monitoring of the Daphne Major finch population, best illustrates how natural selection works?
choix: The large beak took hold once and for all after the 1977 drought, and has never changed since
The direction of selection reversed between 1977 and 1983, depending on whether the available seeds were hard or soft
Large-beaked finches deliberately developed this trait to adapt to the drought
The study could observe selection only in the laboratory, never in the island's wild population
quiz.explication: The 1977 drought favored large beaks, able to crack the hard seeds that remained available; the 1983 El Niño reversed this advantage by making small, soft seeds abundant again, favoring small beaks. The same population showed selection in both directions.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why can the Grants' team measure every finch on Daphne Major rather than a sample?
choix: Because the island's population is small enough to be counted in its entirety
Because the island's finches were all born in captivity and carry an electronic chip
Because the island is closed to all other visitors, which makes banding the birds easier
Because Daphne Major finches never migrate from one season to the next
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text specifies that the island's finch population is small enough to be counted in its entirety, rather than estimated from a sample as is usual elsewhere.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How do the Grants characterize, in a later paper, the evolution observed over several decades on Daphne Major?
choix: As a slow convergence toward an ideal beak form, reached after several decades
As unpredictable evolution: predictable in the short term, but not in the long term because the environment dictating it is not predictable
As strictly cyclical evolution, with an exact return to the same state every six years
As evolution that stopped in the 1980s, the population having not changed since
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Followed over several decades, the population oscillates rather than converges, which leads the Grants to speak of evolution that is unpredictable in the long term, though predictable in the short term.
